Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
• 43-year-old active female with 2-week history of activity-related right knee pain and clicking; clinical picture most consistent with patellofemoral pain syndrome.  

History:
• Presenting complaint: Right knee pain and clicking that begin ~20 min (≈3 mi) into a run; worse with leg-extension/ab exercises; occasionally forces her to stop running.  
• Onset/duration: Started 2 weeks ago after increasing run mileage for marathon training (now 7–8 mi runs).  
• Course/modifying factors: Ice relieved transient swelling after first episode; rest helps; no constant pain at rest.  
• Associated features: Single episode of mild knee swelling (resolved), one episode of right-toe tingling post-run; no locking, giving-way, stiffness, redness, fever, calf pain, or limitation of stairs/walking.  
• Pertinent negatives: No other joint pain, back pain, colour change, persistent oedema.  
• Past medical history: Hyperopia (status post LASIK); prior severe UTI/renal colic work-up; remote right knee bruise from hockey fall months ago; otherwise healthy.  
• Medications: Ibuprofen 400 mg PRN; naproxen (Aleve) PRN; vitamin D; melatonin; occasional Xanax; occasional marijuana smoking.  
• Allergies: Not stated.  
• Social/preventive: Highly active (marathon training, gym, ice hockey); lives in London; no tobacco/alcohol use documented; uses marijuana.  

Examination:
• Remote video only—no formal physical exam performed.  
• Patient reports current knee: no visible swelling, warmth, or redness; full flexion and extension; pain localised “middle then slightly right” of patella; clicking felt during gym leg movements.  
• Gait, stairs, and walking normal per history.  
• Vitals: not recorded.  

Impression:
• Most likely: Patellofemoral pain syndrome (“runner’s knee”) – activity-related anterior/lateral knee pain, clicking, provoked by increased running mileage; normal ROM and stability.  
• Alternative considerations:  
  – Patellar tendinopathy – overuse of extensor mechanism (pain with leg extension).  
  – Degenerative/traumatic meniscal tear – prior hockey trauma and clicking, though lack of locking/effusion lowers likelihood.  

Plan:
• Conservative management: continue regular ice therapy after activity.  
• Activity modification: reduce running intensity/distance until pain-free; avoid painful exercises.  
• Pharmacologic: prescribe stronger NSAID to be taken regularly with food in place of OTC ibuprofen; avoid dual NSAID use.  
• Referral: arrange physiotherapy assessment for detailed knee examination and tailored rehab; imaging (e.g., MRI) considered if poor response or concern for structural injury.  
• Safety-net advice: seek urgent review for persistent or worsening swelling, heat, redness, systemic fever, or if knee locks or cannot be flexed/extended.  
• Follow-up: return or message if symptoms not improving after physiotherapy or within several weeks. Prescription sent to usual pharmacy.  

Quality checks:
● Missing/expected elements: allergies, objective vitals, in-person knee exam, smoking/alcohol history, formal functional assessment.  
● Transcript vs. DDx conflicts: initial patient phrasing “knees” vs later clarification of right knee predominant.  
● Transcript quality: clear history; limited exam possible via video; no background noise; some informal language.
